prompt: Under the CFAA, what actually determines whether accessing a computer system is illegal?
choices: Whether the person intended to cause harm
Whether the person had authorization to access it
Whether the person profited financially from the access
Whether the system contained sensitive data

prompt: Which of the following is explicitly authorized security testing?
choices: Practicing exploits in your own isolated, host-only-networked VM lab
Cracking a neighbor's locked Wi-Fi password because the signal reaches your yard
Running an exploitation tool against a company's login page that is not listed in any bounty scope
Using a friend's streaming account password you found without asking them

prompt: What legally distinguishes a white hat hacker from a black hat hacker?
choices: White hats are more technically skilled
White hats have explicit authorization for what they do; black hats do not
White hats never find real, exploitable vulnerabilities
Black hats only target government systems

prompt: A 'grey hat' hacker scans a company's website without permission, finds a real SQL injection flaw, and reports it with good intentions. What is their legal exposure?
choices: None — reporting the bug afterward retroactively grants authorization
None, as long as they didn't cause measurable damage
They may still be in violation of unauthorized access laws, because the access itself was never authorized
They are automatically entitled to a bug bounty payout

prompt: In a standard coordinated (responsible) disclosure process, when does public disclosure of a vulnerability happen?
choices: Immediately upon discovery, to warn users as fast as possible
Only after the vendor ships a fix, or an agreed-upon timeline (e.g., 90 days) expires
Never — reported vulnerabilities must stay confidential permanently
Only if the vendor agrees to pay a bounty for the report

prompt: A bug bounty scope page lists '*.example.com' as in-scope and explicitly excludes third-party vendor domains and social engineering. Which action stays within scope?
choices: Testing app.example.com (a subdomain of example.com) for an authentication bypass
Calling the company's support line to social-engineer a password reset
Testing a vendor's analytics subdomain hosted on vendor.io
Attempting to physically access the company's server room

prompt: Which treaty is the main international framework harmonizing computer crime laws across many countries, including illegal access and data interference?
choices: The Geneva Convention
The Budapest Convention (Council of Europe Convention on Cybercrime)
The Paris Agreement
The Wassenaar Arrangement

prompt: Which scenario represents authorized access to practice an exploitation technique?
choices: Practicing SQL injection on OWASP Juice Shop, a deliberately vulnerable app built for this purpose
Running automated vulnerability scanners against a random company's production website because it's publicly reachable
Using a friend's email password you discovered without telling them
Brute-forcing a neighbor's Wi-Fi password 'just to see if it's possible'
